teaching_blocks.content: Picture a week's worth of delivery orders for a small courier company: order numbers, the city each order went to, how long the delivery took, which driver handled it. Written down, all of that information becomes what analysts call a dataset -- a collection of observations that are all recorded on the same set of variables. Every delivery in the batch was recorded using the same kind of information: an order number, a city, a delivery time, a driver. That shared structure is what turns a pile of individual facts into one dataset you can work with.

That information is commonly organized as a table -- sometimes called a data matrix -- made of rows and columns. If you opened the delivery-orders file in a spreadsheet, you would see exactly this: a grid where every delivery has its own line, and every piece of information about a delivery has its own column.

The two directions of that grid mean different things. Each row represents one observation -- one record. In the delivery data, that means one row per delivery: order #1042 is one row, order #1043 is the next row, and so on. Each column represents one variable: one attribute that is recorded for every observation in the dataset. So the city column holds the destination city for every single delivery, and the delivery-time column holds the delivery time for every single delivery -- each column holds just one kind of information.

Reading the table this way tells you exactly how to answer a question about it. Asked 'how many deliveries went to Lagos?', you would scan down the city column and count matching rows. Asked 'what happened with order #1042?', you would look across that one row and read every column for it. The row tells you about one delivery; the column tells you about one kind of fact across all deliveries.

This row/column structure is the foundation everything else in analysis builds on: before you can check, clean or make sense of delivery data, you first have to know that a row is one delivery and a column is one attribute of every delivery.

teaching_blocks.content: Back in the delivery-orders table, look at two of its columns: delivery time (say, 32 minutes) and city (say, 'Lagos'). Both are columns in the same table, but they behave completely differently, and knowing which kind of column you're looking at changes what you're allowed to do with it.

A numerical variable takes numerical values for which it is sensible to add or subtract -- delivery time is numerical, because '32 minutes plus 41 minutes' or the difference between two delivery times both mean something real. A categorical variable's values are categories, also called levels -- city is categorical, because its values ('Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Kano') are just labels for a group; there is nothing to add or subtract between them.

A column stored as numbers is not automatically numerical. If arithmetic on the values would be meaningless, the column is categorical even though it looks like numbers. In the delivery data, a zone_code column might hold 101, 102, 103 -- but adding two zone codes together produces nothing useful, the same way adding two telephone area codes would. zone_code is a label, not a quantity, so it's categorical despite being written as digits.

Before doing anything with a column, check which kind it is: can these values be meaningfully added or subtracted, or are they just labels for groups? Getting that distinction right up front decides whether treating that column as a quantity will make sense at all.

teaching_blocks.content: Before trusting any conclusion drawn from the delivery-orders table, you need to ask whether the data itself is any good. Data quality means whether a dataset is fit for the purpose it will be used for -- not whether it looks tidy, but whether it can actually support the question you're asking of it.

Two checks look at what's missing or repeated. Completeness checks whether the records and values that should be present in the dataset actually are, rather than missing -- for example, an order row with no delivery time recorded at all. Uniqueness checks whether a record that should appear only once -- one entity, one row -- is duplicated in the dataset -- for example, the same order number showing up as two separate rows.

Two more checks look at whether the values themselves are trustworthy. Validity checks whether a column's values are in the range and format expected for that column -- a delivery time recorded as '-5 minutes' fails validity, because negative time isn't a valid delivery time. Accuracy checks whether the data correctly matches the real-world thing it describes -- an order logged as delivered to Lagos when the driver actually delivered it to Abuja is complete, unique and validly formatted, but still inaccurate.

Good-quality data does not have to be perfect. The goal of these checks isn't a flawless dataset; it's a dataset good enough to answer the question you actually have, using completeness, uniqueness, validity and accuracy as the specific things to look for.
Running through these checks on the delivery-orders table before analyzing it is what tells you whether you can trust what the numbers say next.

Watching someone scan an actual table and point at a blank cell, a duplicate row, an out-of-range value and a real-world mismatch makes the four checks concrete in a way that describing each one in prose alone doesn't fully convey.

teaching_blocks.content: Once you know how to read the delivery-orders table and check its quality, the next question is what order to actually do things in. A repeatable analysis process typically begins by clarifying the question or purpose -- for the delivery data, that might be 'which cities have unusually slow deliveries?' Clarifying this first means both you and whoever asked for the analysis share an understanding of what is being analyzed and why, before any work starts.

Next comes inspecting and cleaning. Before analysis, the data should be inspected and checked for quality, so problems are addressed as early as possible -- this is where quality checks such as completeness, uniqueness, validity and accuracy from before come in. Cleaning the data then helps reduce quality problems such as duplication and inconsistent values, for example removing the duplicate order row you found during inspection.

With the data prepared, you analyze it: examining the prepared data to answer the question. Exploratory data analysis, for example, looks at the data to uncover its underlying structure and spot anomalies -- unusual values, like one delivery that took far longer than every other delivery in the batch. For the delivery data, analyzing might mean looking closely at the cleaned rows to see which cities' deliveries stand out.

Visualizing is its own step: turning data into plots or other graphics. Exploratory data analysis relies mostly on such graphical techniques to gain insight into a dataset and reveal its structure, but making the graphic is a different job from examining the data. For the delivery data, visualizing might mean turning those delivery times into a graphic so the pattern is easy to see at a glance.

The final stage is communicating the findings, and how far they can be trusted, to the people who will use them -- not merely producing the analysis itself. Telling a manager 'Lagos deliveries are running slow, but the sample is small' is part of the workflow, not an afterthought.

This process is commonly iterative rather than strictly linear: earlier stages, such as inspecting or cleaning, may be revisited as later stages reveal new issues -- if analyzing the delivery data turns up a value that looks wrong, you go back and inspect or clean it before continuing, rather than treating each stage as done for good.

video_need.reason: This is a multi-stage workflow with a loop back into earlier stages -- exactly the kind of process relationship that a diagram of the stages, with the iterative loop drawn in, makes easier to hold in mind than prose describing the same stages in sequence.

teaching_notes: Keep 'analyze' and 'visualize' as clearly distinct steps -- don't let visualize collapse into analyze; this path splits them explicitly.
The iterative note (going back to inspect/clean) should stay a short closing point, not a new sub-workflow.

teaching_blocks.content: The delivery-orders table almost certainly contains information about real people -- customers' addresses, drivers' names. Data users should respect the privacy and confidentiality of the individuals a dataset describes, which means treating that table as more than just numbers to analyze.

Responsible data handling includes minimizing data collection to what is needed and being accountable for how the data is used -- if the analysis only needs delivery times and cities, there's no reason to collect or keep customers' phone numbers. Data work should also consider its potential impact on the people and communities it affects: a finding like 'deliveries to this neighborhood are consistently late' could affect real customers and drivers, not just look interesting in a report.

When sharing data and findings, data users should honestly report data limitations and known biases rather than overstating certainty -- if the delivery data only covers one week, or one driver logged times inconsistently, that limitation belongs in the report, not left out to make the conclusion sound stronger than it is. Identifying information that isn't needed for the purpose should be left out or removed, especially before data is shared; findings can describe a group without identifying individuals -- reporting 'the eastern delivery zone runs slow' rather than naming individual customers.

Removing identifying information does not by itself remove the risk of re-identification: the data, combined with other available data, can still identify people, so removing a name column alone isn't automatically enough.
Treating the people behind the delivery-orders data with care, and being honest about what the analysis can and can't claim, is as much a part of the job as getting the numbers right.

There is no mechanism, tool or changing state to show, so a video would only restate the same points in another voice.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose you're writing code to work with one delivery order and need to keep track of how many minutes it took to arrive. Before you can do anything with that number, you need to store it under a name you can refer back to later. In Python, the equal sign (=) is used to assign a value to a variable, so delivery_minutes = 32 stores the value 32 under the name delivery_minutes.

A name only exists once something has been assigned to it. Trying to use a name before assigning it a value -- referring to average_delivery_minutes before any earlier line has assigned it something -- raises a NameError, rather than quietly giving back some default value.

Assigning to a name that already holds a value doesn't create a second value alongside the first: it rebinds the name to the new value, replacing what it held. If delivery_minutes = 32 is followed later by a corrected delivery_minutes = 45, the name delivery_minutes now refers to 45 instead of 32.

Not every word can be a variable name. A valid name is made of letters, digits and the underscore, cannot start with a digit, is case-significant (so delivery_minutes and Delivery_Minutes are two different names), and cannot be one of Python's reserved keywords, such as if, for or class -- those are reserved for Python's own syntax.

Once a name holds a value, later code can use it in an expression, the same way the value 20 assigned to width and 5 * 9 assigned to height let a later line compute width * height. In a delivery context, after orders_per_driver = 20 and days_worked = 5, a later line such as orders_per_driver * days_worked reads back both stored values and computes a result from them.
= stores a value under a name, assigning again to that same name replaces what it held, and using a name that was never assigned raises an error instead of producing a value.

teaching_blocks.content: Every value in Python has a type. In delivery data, an order id like 1042, a delivery time like 32.5, a city name like 'Lagos', and whether an order was late are four different kinds of value -- Python has a core scalar type for each kind.

Integer literals -- whole numbers written without a decimal point, such as 2, 4, or 20 -- have type int. A literal written with a fractional part, such as 5.0 or 1.6, has type float. So order_id = 1042 is an int, while delivery_minutes = 32.5 is a float.
Text values are of type str, and they can be written with either single quotes or double quotes with the same result -- city = 'Lagos' and city = "Lagos" create the identical string value.
The bool type has exactly two values, True and False -- for example, is_late = True records whether a delivery ran late, and there is no third bool value.
print() writes out the value of its arguments, and when that value is a string, print() writes it without the surrounding quotes -- print(city) displays Lagos, not 'Lagos'.

The built-in type() function, called with one argument, returns the type of that object -- print(type(delivery_minutes)) shows <class 'float'>, and print(type(city)) shows <class 'str'>, letting you check a value's type directly instead of guessing from how it was written.
The takeaway: 1042, 32.5, 'Lagos' and True are four different kinds of value -- int, float, str and bool -- and type() tells you which one a value is.

teaching_blocks.content: The operators +, -, * and / perform addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, and / always returns a float, even when both operands are whole numbers. // performs floor division, discarding the fractional part, and % returns the remainder of the division -- 17 // 5 is 3 and 17 % 5 is 2; ** calculates a power, so 5 ** 2 is 5 squared.

Parentheses can be used to group an expression and control how it is evaluated, e.g. (delivery_minutes + wait_minutes) * 2. Mixing an int and a float in one of these operators converts the integer operand to floating point first -- 4 * 3.75 - 1 evaluates to 14.0, not 14.

teaching_blocks.content: Comparing two values in code is how a question like 'is this delivery late?' turns into something a program can act on. The standard comparison operators are <, <=, >, >=, == and !=.

A comparison evaluates to a boolean value, True or False -- for example 3 < 5 evaluates to True. Applied to delivery data, delivery_minutes > 60 evaluates to True for an order that took more than 60 minutes, and False otherwise.
Any of the six operators works the same way: delivery_minutes == 0 checks for an exact match, and city != 'Lagos' checks for a mismatch.
A comparison like delivery_minutes > 60 evaluates to one of the two bool values, True or False.

teaching_notes: Skip chained comparisons (optional f3) unless there's room -- it's enrichment, not required.

teaching_blocks.content: A single comparison like delivery_minutes > 60 only asks one question at a time. Combining more than one condition -- 'is this delivery both late and far from the depot?' -- needs Python's logical operators.

The Boolean operations, in ascending order of priority, are or, and, and not. Priority decides how a mixed expression is grouped when there are no parentheses: and has higher priority than or, so is_late or is_far and is_first_week is read as is_late or (is_far and is_first_week).

x or y evaluates to x if x is true, otherwise to y. or is a short-circuit operator: it only evaluates y if x turns out to be false -- so is_late or is_far only checks is_far once is_late has come back false.

x and y evaluates to x if x is false, otherwise to y. and is also short-circuit: it only evaluates y if x turns out to be true -- so is_late and is_far only checks is_far once is_late has already come back true.

not x evaluates to True if x is false, and False if x is true -- not is_late flips whichever value is_late holds. not has a lower priority than the comparison operators, so not delivery_minutes == 0 is interpreted as not (delivery_minutes == 0).

A rule like 'flag this delivery if it's late or unusually far' reads directly as is_late or is_far, and a stricter rule like 'flag it only if it's late and it's the driver's first week' reads as is_late and is_first_week. With is_late = False and is_far = True, is_late or is_far evaluates to True, and is_late and is_far evaluates to False without checking is_far.
and, or and not let you build one compound condition out of several simpler comparisons.

teaching_blocks.content: Data often arrives as the wrong type for what you want to do with it -- a delivery time typed into a form as the text '32' rather than the number 32. The constructors int() and float() can be used to produce a number of a specific type from another value.
int(string) returns an integer object constructed from a string -- int('123') returns 123.
float(string) returns a floating-point number constructed from a string -- float('+1.23') returns 1.23.
Strings may also be created from other objects using the str constructor -- so str(32) turns the integer 32 into the string '32'.

Not every string can be converted this way. float(string) requires the string to conform to a specific numeric format -- an optional sign and digits, optionally with a decimal point or exponent, after surrounding whitespace is removed. A string that isn't in the format the target type accepts raises an error: for int(), a string that isn't a plain integer, such as int('3.5'), raises a ValueError.
Converting a string to a number only works when the string matches the format the target type accepts -- otherwise the conversion raises a ValueError instead of guessing.

teaching_blocks.content: Keeping five separate variables for five delivery times gets unwieldy fast. A list groups values together in one ordered collection: it's written as a comma-separated sequence of values inside square brackets, e.g. delivery_times = [32, 45, 21, 60, 18].

Lists can be indexed and sliced. delivery_times[0] returns the first item (32), and delivery_times[-1] returns the last item (18); a slice such as delivery_times[-3:] returns a new list of the last three items ([21, 60, 18]).
In a slice such as delivery_times[1:3], the start index is included and the end index is excluded, so it returns [45, 21] -- the items from index 1 up to but not including index 3.
Lists are mutable: an item can be replaced in place. delivery_times[3] = 50 changes the value stored at index 3 from 60 to 50, without creating a new list.
New items can be added to the end of a list with the list.append() method -- delivery_times.append(27) adds a sixth delivery time onto the end of the list.
The built-in function len() returns the number of items in a list, so len(delivery_times) tells you how many deliveries are currently in the collection.
A list keeps an ordered group of values under one name, lets you reach any item by position, and can grow or change in place as new delivery data comes in.

teaching_blocks.content: Sometimes what you need isn't a plain ordered list but a lookup by key. A dictionary is a collection of key: value pairs, written inside braces, where the keys must be unique within the dictionary -- order_city = {1042: 'Lagos', 1043: 'Abuja'} maps each order id to the city it was delivered to.

A value is stored or updated by assigning to a key, e.g. order_city[1044] = 'Kano' adds a new order, and retrieved by subscripting with the key, e.g. order_city[1042] returns 'Lagos'. Updating a key the same way replaces its value -- order_city[1042] = 'Ibadan' replaces 'Lagos' with 'Ibadan' for that order.
Extracting a value for a key that is not in the dictionary by subscripting raises a KeyError -- order_city[9999] fails if no order 9999 was ever added.
The get() method returns None (or a specified default value) instead of raising an error when a key is not in the dictionary, so order_city.get(9999) returns None rather than crashing.
The in keyword checks whether a key is present in a dictionary, e.g. 1042 in order_city is True.
A dictionary looks values up by key instead of by position, which is exactly what you need when 'find the city for this order id' matters more than 'what's the third item.'

teaching_blocks.content: Sometimes you want to group a small, fixed set of values together, rather than a list, which can grow as you append to it. A tuple consists of a number of values separated by commas; its items are shown enclosed in parentheses on output, and a tuple may be written with or without surrounding parentheses as input, e.g. order = 1042, 'Lagos', 32 (equivalently order = (1042, 'Lagos', 32)).
Tuples are immutable: once created, an item inside a tuple cannot be reassigned -- order[0] = 1099 raises a TypeError.
A tuple can be unpacked into several variables at once, e.g. order_id, city, minutes = order, provided there are as many variables as there are elements in the tuple.
Enclosing a single value in parentheses does not make it a tuple -- singleton = ('Lagos') is still just the string 'Lagos'. A one-item tuple needs a trailing comma instead, e.g. singleton = 'Lagos',.
A tuple groups a fixed set of values whose items can't be reassigned one by one, and unpacking hands each piece back to its own name when you need to work with it on its own.

teaching_blocks.content: Sometimes you only care about which distinct values appear -- which cities orders were delivered to, with no duplicates. A set is an unordered collection with no duplicate elements, used for membership testing and eliminating duplicate entries.
Curly braces or the set() function create a set -- but set() must be used for an empty set, because {} creates an empty dictionary instead.

set() can also build a set from the items of another collection, e.g. cities = set(['Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Lagos', 'Kano']) produces {'Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Kano'} -- the set of unique cities, with the repeated 'Lagos' collapsed to one. The order the items print in may differ from the order they were added, since a set is unordered.

The in operator tests membership in a set, e.g. 'Lagos' in cities checks whether 'Lagos' is one of the cities in the set -- with cities = set(['Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Lagos', 'Kano']), 'Lagos' in cities is True.

Set objects support mathematical operations such as union (a | b) and intersection (a & b) -- if week1_cities and week2_cities are two sets of cities, week1_cities & week2_cities gives the cities that appear in both weeks, and week1_cities | week2_cities gives every city that appears in either week.
A set fits when duplicates don't matter and all you need is which distinct values are present, or whether one value is present at all.

teaching_blocks.content: A quote character can be embedded in a string without escaping it by enclosing the string in the other kind of quote instead: writing "This delivery wasn't late" inside double quotes needs no escaping, where the same text inside single quotes would need the apostrophe escaped, e.g. 'This delivery wasn\'t late'.

An f-string is a string literal prefixed with f or F that embeds the value of a Python expression inside the string by writing the expression in curly brackets {expression} -- f"Delivery to {city} took {delivery_minutes} minutes" substitutes in the current values of city and delivery_minutes.

An optional format specifier can follow the expression after a colon, giving greater control over how the value is formatted, such as rounding a number to a chosen number of places after the decimal, e.g. f"Average: {avg_minutes:.2f} minutes" produces the string 'Average: 32.67 minutes' when avg_minutes is 32.666.
f-strings let you build one readable message out of literal text and live variable values, with the format specifier controlling exactly how a number like a delivery time is displayed.

teaching_blocks.content: Not every line of code should always run -- sometimes what happens next depends on the data. An if statement executes its block only when its condition is true.
There can be zero or more elif parts after an if, and the else part is optional; elif is short for 'else if' and helps avoid excessive indentation from nested if statements.
An if/elif/.../else chain selects exactly one block by evaluating the conditions one by one until one is found to be true; if none of them are true, the else block (if present) is executed.
Reading top to bottom, exactly one branch of an if/elif/else chain runs for any given delivery time -- the first whose condition is true, or else if none are.

teaching_blocks.content: Once delivery times are collected in a list, you'll want to do something with every single one of them, not just one at a time by hand. Python's for statement iterates over the items of any sequence, such as a list or a string, in the order that they appear in the sequence.

Each pass through a for loop binds the loop variable to the next item of the sequence:
for minutes in delivery_times:
    print(minutes)
This prints every delivery time in delivery_times, one per pass.
A for loop visits every item of a sequence such as a list once, in the order the items appear, which is what you need to process each delivery time in turn.

video_need.reason: Watching the loop variable take on each item one pass at a time makes the binding behavior concrete, though the worked delivery_times example already traces through it precisely.

teaching_blocks.content: Sometimes you don't know in advance how many times you'll need to repeat something -- you just want to keep going as long as some condition holds. A while loop executes its body repeatedly as long as its condition remains true; the condition can be a comparison, such as a < 10.

The body of a while loop is indented beneath it, and something in the body has to change what the condition checks:
a, b = 0, 1
while a < 10:
    print(a)
    a, b = b, a+b
Each pass prints a, then a, b = b, a+b updates a. The loop prints 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 and stops once a < 10 becomes false (a has reached 13).

Applied to delivery data:
pending = 3
while pending > 0:
    print('deliveries left:', pending)
    pending = pending - 1
Each pass prints the current count and then decreases pending by 1, so the loop stops once pending reaches 0.

Unlike a for loop, which is bound to a known collection, a while loop keeps running purely based on its condition, so the code inside it must eventually make that condition false or the loop never stops.

teaching_blocks.content: The break statement breaks out of the innermost enclosing for or while loop -- useful for stopping a search over delivery orders as soon as the one you want is found.

The continue statement continues with the next iteration of the loop, skipping the rest of the current one -- for example, skipping a delivery record that's missing a time without exiting the whole loop.

teaching_blocks.content: Building a new list from an existing one by looping, one item at a time, is common enough that Python has a shorthand for it. A list comprehension consists of brackets containing an expression followed by a for clause, and optionally more for or if clauses; it produces a new list from evaluating the expression in that context -- [minutes * 2 for minutes in delivery_times] doubles each value in delivery_times.
A list comprehension can filter its source with an if clause, e.g. [minutes for minutes in delivery_times if minutes >= 45] keeps only the delivery times that satisfy that condition.
Dict comprehensions create dictionaries from arbitrary key and value expressions, e.g. {city: len(city) for city in ('Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Kano')} maps each city name to the length of its name.
A comprehension does in one line what a for loop with an if check and an empty list to append into would otherwise take several lines to build.

video_need.reason: The bracket-expression-for-if skeleton is a fixed pattern that the worked delivery_times and city examples already demonstrate completely.

teaching_blocks.content: You've already looped over lists with for. Looping over other collections follows the same for x in ... pattern, but what you get back per pass differs by collection. Looping directly over a dictionary (for x in d) yields its keys -- for order_id in order_city: visits each order id, not each city.
When looping through a dictionary, the key and its corresponding value can be retrieved together using the items() method, e.g. for order_id, city in order_city.items(): print(order_id, city).

A set's elements may come out in a different order than expected when iterated over, because a set is unordered -- looping over a set of cities won't necessarily visit them in the order they were added.
Tuples are a sequence type, so a for loop visits their items in order the same way it does for a list -- for value in order: visits 1042, then 'Lagos', then 32, when order = (1042, 'Lagos', 32).

The same for x in ... syntax works across lists, dicts, sets and tuples -- what changes is what each pass hands you (an item, a key, or, with .items(), a key-value pair), and for a set the order isn't guaranteed.

teaching_blocks.content: Repeating the same block of code for every delivery record gets tedious to copy and paste. The keyword def introduces a function definition, followed by the function's name and a parenthesized, possibly empty, list of parameter names, e.g. def summarize_delivery():; the statements forming the body start on the next line and must be indented.
A function definition associates the function name with the function object; calling the function by that name (e.g. summarize_delivery()) runs its body.

For example:
def summarize_delivery():
    print('--- delivery summary ---')

summarize_delivery()
summarize_delivery()
The def block only defines the function; its body runs when the function is called. Each call runs the same body again, so this prints the line twice without retyping the print().
def creates a reusable block of code under a name; calling that name followed by parentheses is what actually runs it.

teaching_blocks.content: A function that always does exactly the same thing on every call is limited. The formal parameters of a function are named in its def statement's parenthesized list -- def classify_delivery(minutes): names one parameter, minutes.

Inside the function body, each parameter name refers to the argument value that was passed for it when the function was called -- inside classify_delivery, minutes refers to whatever value was passed in that particular call.

When a function is called with positional arguments, if there are N positional arguments, they are placed in the function's first N parameter slots, in order -- for def delivery_summary(city, minutes):, calling delivery_summary('Lagos', 32) places 'Lagos' into the city slot and 32 into the minutes slot.
Parameters name the inputs a function expects; the arguments in a specific call supply the actual values for that one run.

teaching_blocks.content: Printing a result from inside a function shows it once, but the caller can't reuse it afterward. A return statement sends a value back to the code that called the function -- return category gives the caller access to that value instead of just displaying it.

Even a function without a return statement does return a value: the built-in value None. So a function that only prints something, without an explicit return, hands back None to its caller, not the thing it printed -- for example:
def show(m):
    print(m)

x = show(5)
This prints 5, and x itself is None.

The returned value can be stored in a variable for later use -- result = classify_delivery(32) stores whatever classify_delivery returns in result, so later code can reuse result without calling the function again.
return is what turns a function from something that just does an action into something that hands back a result the rest of your code can store and reuse.

teaching_blocks.content: Specifying a default value for a parameter, e.g. def ask_ok(prompt, retries=4):, creates a function that can be called with fewer arguments than it's defined to accept -- ask_ok('Delete this order?') works, using 4 for retries.
A function can also be called using keyword arguments of the form kwarg=value, e.g. ask_ok(prompt='Delete this order?', retries=2); in a call, keyword arguments must follow any positional arguments.
All the keyword arguments passed in a call must match one of the function's parameters, and no parameter may receive a value more than once.

A default value is evaluated only once, at the point the function is defined, not on each call. If that default is a mutable object such as a list, the same object is shared across calls and can accumulate changes unless the function is written to create a fresh value each time.

teaching_blocks.content: A variable created inside a function doesn't automatically become visible outside it. All variable assignments in a function store the value in that function's local symbol table.

For a function that is not nested inside another function, variable references inside it first look in the local symbol table, then the global symbol table, and finally the table of built-in names -- so a name assigned only outside the function is still readable inside it, found in the global table once the local lookup fails.

A global variable cannot be directly assigned a value from inside a function unless it is named in a global statement; it may still be referenced (read) without such a statement. A function that does total = 0 while a global total already exists, without first writing global total, creates a new local total instead of updating the global one -- the global total keeps its old value.

This is why a same-named local can shadow a global inside a function without disturbing the global's value outside it -- reading the name inside the function sees the local one, while code outside the function still sees the unchanged global.
Assigning to a name inside a function makes it local by default; only reading (not assigning) reaches out to a global with the same name, unless a global statement says otherwise.

teaching_blocks.content: Code that might fail -- like converting text a user typed into a number -- shouldn't crash the whole program over one bad input. The try statement first executes the statements in its try clause; if no exception occurs, the except clause is skipped and execution of the try statement finishes.
If an exception occurs during the try clause and its type matches the exception named after except, the except clause is executed and execution continues after the try/except block.
try/except lets the program attempt something that might fail and respond to the specific failure, rather than stopping entirely.

teaching_blocks.content: Not all functionality needs to be written from scratch inside one file. A module is a file containing Python definitions and statements; definitions from a module can be imported into another module or into the main script with the import statement, e.g. import fibo.
Importing a module this way does not add the names defined in it directly to the current namespace -- it adds the module name, so its functions are accessed through that name, e.g. fibo.fib(1000).

The from module import name variant imports names from a module directly into the importing module's namespace, e.g. from fibo import fib, so it can then be called as fib(500) without the module prefix.
Python comes with a library of standard modules that are imported the same way, e.g. import sys makes the sys module's names, such as sys.path, available through sys.
import gives you access to code written in another file -- either through the module's name (import fibo, fibo.fib(...)) or directly by name (from fibo import fib, fib(...)).

teaching_blocks.content: Delivery records don't always start out inside your running program -- they might live in a text or CSV file on disk. open(filename, mode) returns a file object; mode can be 'r' to read, 'w' to write (erasing an existing file of the same name), or 'a' to append, and 'r' is assumed if mode is omitted.

It's good practice to use the with keyword when working with a file object, because it closes the file automatically after its block finishes, even if an exception is raised -- with open('orders.txt') as f: ....
f.read() reads a file's contents and returns them as a string in text mode; once the end of the file is reached, further calls to f.read() return an empty string.
csv.DictReader(f) creates a reader that maps each row of a CSV file to a dict, using the first row's values as keys by default, e.g. for row in reader: print(row['city'], row['delivery_minutes']).
f.write(string) writes the contents of string to the file, returning the number of characters written.

csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=['order_id', 'city']) creates a writer that maps a dict to a row; writer.writeheader() writes the header row and writer.writerow(dict) writes one data row, in the order given by fieldnames.
A CSV file used with the csv module should be opened with newline='', e.g. open('orders.csv', 'w', newline='').

Put together:
import csv

with open('orders.csv', newline='') as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    for row in reader:
        print(row['order_id'], row['city'])

with open('lagos_orders.csv', 'w', newline='') as out:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(out, fieldnames=['order_id', 'city'])
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerow({'order_id': 1042, 'city': 'Lagos'})
If orders.csv starts with the header order_id,city,delivery_minutes, each row is a dict with those keys, so row['city'] reads that row's city. The second block creates lagos_orders.csv (erasing any existing file of that name) containing the header order_id,city and the row 1042,Lagos. Both files close automatically when their with blocks end.

Reading and writing files is how a program's delivery data gets in from, and results get out to, storage that outlives the program run -- open() and with manage the connection, and the csv module adds row/column structure on top of plain text.

teaching_blocks.content: PEP 8 recommends using 4 spaces per indentation level, with spaces rather than tabs as the preferred indentation method, and limiting all lines to a maximum of 79 characters.

PEP 8 recommends avoiding extraneous whitespace, such as immediately inside parentheses, brackets or braces, or immediately before a comma, semicolon, or colon -- e.g. spam(ham[1], {eggs: 2}) rather than spam( ham[ 1 ], { eggs: 2 } ).
PEP 8 recommends that function and variable names be lowercase, with words separated by underscores as necessary for readability -- delivery_minutes rather than deliveryMinutes or DeliveryMinutes.
These are recommendations for readability: following them makes code easier to read for the next person -- including a later you.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a batch of seven delivery orders whose delivery times, in minutes, are 18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, and 80. Before you can say anything useful about this batch, you need one number that answers "what's typical here?" -- and there are three different ways to compute that number.

The sample mean is computed as the sum of the observed values divided by the number of observations. For the seven delivery times, the sum is 18+20+22+22+26+28+80 = 216, and 216 divided by 7 is about 30.9 minutes.

The median is the middle value when the data are ordered from smallest to largest; if there is an even number of observations, the median is the average of the two middle values. Sorted, the seven times are 18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, 80 -- the middle (fourth) value is 22 minutes.
The mode is the value that occurs most often in the data; there can be more than one mode. In this batch, 22 minutes appears twice while every other value appears once, so 22 is the mode.

Notice that the mean (about 30.9 minutes) sits well above the median and mode (both 22 minutes). That gap exists because the mean is more strongly affected by extreme observations (such as those in the tail of a skewed distribution) than the median, which is more robust to them; for this reason the median can better represent a typical value in a skewed dataset. Here, the single 80-minute delivery pulls the mean upward far more than it moves the median, so 22 minutes -- not 30.9 -- is the more representative "typical" delivery time for this batch.

Mean, median, and mode all try to answer "what's typical," but they compute it differently, and the mean and median react differently to a batch that includes one unusually large value -- so before reporting a single center number, it's worth checking whether an extreme value like that 80-minute delivery is pulling the mean away from where most of the data actually sits.

teaching_notes: The dataset (18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, 80 minutes) is reused across measures of center and spread for continuity -- keep the sum (216), mean (~30.9), median (22), and mode (22) consistent everywhere they reappear.

The word 'skewed' above is used only in the informal sense the brief's own fact (f4) already uses it in, not as a defined term.

teaching_blocks.content: Knowing the typical delivery time (22 minutes, from the median) doesn't say how spread out the batch is. Most of the seven delivery times (18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, 80 minutes) cluster fairly close together, but one sits far away -- spread measures capture that difference.
The range of a data set is the largest value minus the smallest value. For this batch, that's 80 minus 18, or 62 minutes.

The variance is computed by taking each observation's deviation from the mean, squaring it, summing the squared deviations, and dividing by n - 1 (one less than the number of observations); it is roughly the average squared distance of the observations from the mean. With a mean of about 30.9 minutes, the seven squared deviations sum to about 2886.9, and dividing by n - 1 = 6 gives a variance of about 481.1 (in minutes squared).

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, and it describes the typical distance of an observation from the mean. The square root of about 481.1 is about 21.9 minutes -- roughly how far a typical delivery time sits from the 30.9-minute mean.

The standard deviation is expressed in the same units as the original data, while the variance is expressed in squared units; the range is based only on the two most extreme values and ignores how the rest of the data are spread. That's why "about 21.9 minutes" (the standard deviation) is easier to interpret directly than "about 481.1 minutes squared" (the variance) -- and why the range (62 minutes) says nothing about whether the other five delivery times are bunched tightly or scattered widely.

Range, variance, and standard deviation all quantify spread, but the range only looks at the two extremes, while variance and standard deviation take every observation's distance from the mean into account -- with standard deviation, unlike variance, expressed in the original units, and so usually the easiest to talk about in context.

teaching_blocks.content: Look at a different batch of delivery times, this one trailing off gradually: 18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, 34, 41, 52 minutes. Most of the batch sits bunched between 18 and 28 minutes, and the remaining values increase step by step rather than jumping straight to one far-off value. That overall pattern -- where the bulk of the values sit and which direction, if any, the data trails off toward -- is what analysts call the shape of a distribution.

A distribution is right-skewed when it has a longer tail trailing off to the right, and left-skewed when it has a longer tail trailing off to the left. This delivery-time batch is right-skewed: the bulk of the values sit between 18 and 28 minutes, and 34, 41, and 52 form a gradually lengthening tail trailing off to the right.

A distribution is symmetric when it trails off by roughly equal amounts in both directions. If the batch instead had values spread evenly above and below its center -- say some deliveries a bit faster and some a bit slower than 24 minutes, with no single value trailing far off in either direction -- that would be a symmetric distribution instead.

The mean is more affected by extreme observations, such as those in the long tail of a skewed distribution, than the median, which is more robust to them. That's consistent with this batch: its mean (about 29.2 minutes) sits above its median (26 minutes), pulled upward by the gradual right-hand tail.

Describing a distribution's shape -- symmetric, right-skewed, or left-skewed -- is about how the bulk of the values are arranged around the center and which direction, if any, a long tail points; it's a separate description from picking out any one extreme value by itself.

teaching_blocks.content: In the same delivery-time batch (18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, 80 minutes), that 80-minute order stands out from the rest. An outlier is an observation that appears extreme relative to the rest of the data -- and that single delivery clearly qualifies.

Examining a dataset for outliers can help identify strong skew in the distribution, spot possible data collection or data entry errors, and reveal interesting properties of the data. For that 80-minute order, this could mean noticing the skew it creates, checking whether someone mistyped "8.0" as "80," or discovering something genuinely unusual, like the delivery being stuck behind a road closure.

Examine an outlier to judge whether it is a possible data collection or data entry error or a genuine observation; a genuine outlier should not be removed without a very good reason. That means checking the order record itself -- was 80 actually logged, or should it have been 8.0? -- before deciding what to do about it.

An outlier is not automatically a data error: it may instead be a genuine, correct observation. If the driver really did take 80 minutes because of a road closure, that's real information about that specific delivery -- not something to delete just because the value looks unusual next to the rest of the batch.
Spotting the extreme value is only the first step; reasoning about why it's there -- an error to fix, or a genuine event worth understanding -- is what actually decides what to do with it.

teaching_blocks.content: Instead of listing every delivery time one by one, imagine grouping a full day's 21 deliveries into 10-minute ranges and counting how many orders fall into each range.

A histogram groups numerical values into bins and represents the count of observations in each bin as a bar; taller bars show where the data values are relatively more common. For the day's 21 deliveries, the tallest bar would sit over the 20-30 minute bin, and a much shorter bar would sit far out over the 80-90 minute bin.

The table of counts of observations in each bin, which a histogram displays as bars, is called a frequency table. For that same day, the frequency table might read: 10-20 minutes, 4 orders; 20-30 minutes, 9 orders; 30-40 minutes, 5 orders; 40-50 minutes, 2 orders; 50-80 minutes, 0 orders; 80-90 minutes, 1 order.

A mode appears in a histogram as a prominent peak: a bin, or region of neighboring bins, where observations are noticeably more concentrated than elsewhere. In the frequency table above, the 20-30 minute bin, with 9 of the 21 orders, is that peak.

Reading a histogram or frequency table means translating bar heights, or bin counts, back into statements about the data: where deliveries cluster most, and where the rare, far-out ones sit -- in this case, a strong cluster around 20-30 minutes with a single delivery trailing far out past 80 minutes.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose two numeric columns are recorded for many delivery orders: distance in kilometers, and delivery time in minutes. Do longer distances tend to go with longer delivery times?
Correlation, which always takes values between -1 and 1, describes the strength of the linear relationship between two numeric variables.

In a positive association, higher values of one variable tend to go with higher values of the other; in a negative association, higher values of one variable tend to go with lower values of the other. For distance and delivery time, a positive association would mean farther orders tend to take longer; a negative association would look different -- for example, if drivers-on-shift and delivery time have a correlation of about -0.65, that means more drivers on shift tends to go with shorter delivery times.

A correlation near +1 indicates a strong positive linear relationship, a correlation near -1 indicates a strong negative linear relationship, and a correlation near 0 indicates little or no linear relationship. Suppose the correlation between distance and delivery time in this dataset comes out to 0.82 -- close to +1, so distance and delivery time have a strong positive linear relationship: farther deliveries tend to take longer.

Correlation quantifies the strength of a linear relationship only; a nonlinear relationship can be strong even when its correlation value looks weak. So a correlation near 0 between two variables doesn't automatically mean they're unrelated -- it may mean their relationship isn't a straight-line one.
Reading a correlation value means reading its sign for direction and how close it sits to -1, 0, or +1 for strength -- without needing to recompute anything from the raw data yourself.

teaching_notes: Skip the optional fact that r is exactly -1/+1 only for a perfectly linear relationship -- not required.
The correlation value (0.82) here is illustrative, matching the assessment_target's framing of reading an already-given coefficient rather than computing one from raw data.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose three numeric variables are recorded for the same delivery orders -- distance in kilometers, package weight in kilograms, and delivery time in minutes -- and their pairwise correlations come out to: distance and delivery time, 0.82; weight and delivery time, -0.41; distance and weight, -0.38.

The strength of a correlation is judged by its magnitude (absolute value): the closer the value is to 1, the stronger the linear relationship, regardless of whether the sign is positive or negative. Comparing the three values above by magnitude, 0.82 (distance and delivery time) is the strongest relationship and -0.38 (distance and weight) is the weakest -- even though -0.41 (weight and delivery time) is the lowest number of the three, its magnitude makes it slightly stronger than -0.38.

A confounding variable is a variable that is correlated with both of two other variables being studied, so it can produce an association between those two variables that is not a direct link between them. Here, distance is correlated with both weight and delivery time -- farther orders might tend to be lighter parcels, and also tend to take longer -- so the -0.41 correlation between weight and delivery time doesn't by itself mean weight and delivery time are directly linked; distance could be behind both.

Comparing magnitudes across a set of correlations tells you which relationships are relatively stronger or weaker, but a strong pairwise correlation on its own never rules out a third variable driving both sides of that pair.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose an analysis finds that orders placed with the delivery app's "priority" toggle switched on correlate with faster delivery times.

Association does not imply causation: a correlation between two variables does not by itself establish that one causes the other. Finding that priority orders and fast deliveries move together in the data doesn't by itself prove that flipping the toggle is what speeds things up.

When only observational (correlational) data supports a finding, it should be restated as an association, or as a hypothesis to check later, rather than as a causal claim. So instead of writing "using priority delivery causes faster delivery," the honest version is closer to "priority orders and faster delivery times tend to occur together in this data; whether the toggle itself speeds things up is worth checking further" -- since, for example, priority orders might simply tend to come from closer neighborhoods.
Before writing up a correlational finding, check whether the wording claims a cause; if the data is only observational, restate it as an association instead of a causal claim.

teaching_blocks.content: Every pandas table starts from two building blocks. A pandas Series is a one-dimensional labeled array that can hold data of any type; its axis labels are collectively called the index.

A pandas Series can be constructed from data that is array-like, an Iterable (such as a Python list), a dict, or a scalar value. When built from a list (or other array-like data) with no index passed, the index defaults to 0, 1, ..., len(data) - 1; when built from a dict, the dict's keys become the index. `pd.Series([18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, 80])` -- built from a plain Python list of delivery times with no index passed -- defaults its labels to 0, 1, ..., 6. `pd.Series({"Lagos": 18, "Abuja": 20, "Kano": 26})`, built from a dict, instead uses "Lagos", "Abuja", and "Kano" as the index.
A pandas DataFrame is a two-dimensional labeled data structure whose columns can hold different types, and it can be thought of as a dict of Series objects that share an index.

A DataFrame can be constructed from a dict of equal-length lists, where each key becomes a column name and each list becomes that column's values: `orders = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [1001, 1002, 1003], "city": ["Lagos", "Abuja", "Kano"], "delivery_time_minutes": [18, 20, 26]})` builds a three-column, three-row orders table this way.

A DataFrame can be treated like a dict of like-indexed Series: `df['col']` gets a column, and `df['new'] = ...` sets (or adds) a column, using the same syntax as the analogous dict operations. `orders['city']` gets the city column back as a Series, and `orders['courier'] = ['Ada', 'Bayo', 'Chidi']` adds a new column, using exactly the syntax you'd use to read or write a dict entry.

A DataFrame's column, once pulled out with `orders['delivery_time_minutes']`, is itself a Series -- the same one-dimensional, indexed structure this concept started with, now sharing the DataFrame's index.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose your delivery records arrive as a CSV export or an Excel workbook. Before pandas can work with them, you read the file into a DataFrame.
read_csv() is the main pandas function for reading a delimited text file, such as a CSV file, into a DataFrame: `orders = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")`.
read_excel() reads an Excel file (such as a .xlsx workbook) into a DataFrame: `orders = pd.read_excel("orders.xlsx", sheet_name="January")`.

read_csv() takes the file path (or URL) to read as its first argument, and read_excel() additionally takes a sheet_name argument to choose which sheet of the workbook to load -- which is why the Excel example above names "January" but the CSV example doesn't need to.

read_csv() accepts arguments such as sep to change the field delimiter used to parse the file (the default is a comma). If a delivery export instead used semicolons, `pd.read_csv("orders.csv", sep=";")` reads it correctly.
Whichever reader you call, once the file is loaded successfully you have a DataFrame ready to work with -- what to check inside it comes next.

teaching_blocks.content: Not every DataFrame starts life as a file -- sometimes delivery data already exists as Python data, and you build the table directly from it.

A DataFrame can be constructed from a dict of equal-length lists, where each key becomes a column name and each list becomes that column's values; if no index is passed, the result uses a default range index: `orders = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [1001, 1002, 1003], "city": ["Lagos", "Abuja", "Kano"]})`.

A DataFrame can also be constructed from a list of dicts, where each dict becomes one row and the dict keys become the column names: `orders = pd.DataFrame([{"order_id": 1001, "city": "Lagos"}, {"order_id": 1002, "city": "Abuja"}, {"order_id": 1003, "city": "Kano"}])` builds the same kind of table one row at a time instead.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose you want the city and delivery time for a particular order, or the first three rows regardless of their labels -- pandas gives two different accessors depending on how you want to address the data.
.loc selects data primarily by label (row or column names), while .iloc selects data primarily by integer position, from 0 to length-1 of the axis.

Both .loc and .iloc select using a row selector and a column selector separated by a comma (e.g. df.loc[rows, cols]); an axis left out of the selection, or given as a colon (:), means "all of that axis", so `orders.loc[3]` is equivalent to `orders.loc[3, :]` -- both return every column for the row labeled 3.
`orders.loc[2:4, "city"]` selects the city column for the rows labeled 2 through 4.

.loc slicing with labels (e.g. 'a':'f') includes both the start and the stop labels in the result, unlike ordinary Python slicing where the stop is excluded. So `orders.loc[2:4]` returns the rows labeled 2, 3, and 4 -- three rows, not two.
`orders.iloc[0:3, 0:2]` selects, by pure position, the first three rows and first two columns.

.iloc uses 0-based positional indexing where, when slicing, the start position is included and the stop position is excluded, following ordinary Python/NumPy slicing rules. So `orders.iloc[0:3]` returns positions 0, 1, and 2 -- three rows, matching normal Python slicing behavior.

The boundary rule flips between the two accessors -- .loc's label slices include the stop label, .iloc's position slices exclude the stop position -- which is worth double-checking any time a slice's row count looks off by one.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose you only want the delivery orders that took longer than 25 minutes.

Comparing a DataFrame column with a value (e.g. df['A'] > 0) produces a True/False Series of the same length as the column, which can be used directly inside the DataFrame's [] to keep only the matching rows (e.g. df[df['A'] > 0]): `orders[orders["delivery_time_minutes"] > 25]` keeps only the slower deliveries.

You may select rows from a DataFrame using a boolean vector the same length as the DataFrame's index; only the rows where the vector is True are kept -- which is exactly what happened above: every row lined up with a True in that comparison came through, every row lined up with a False was dropped.

When combining multiple boolean conditions with the operators | (or), & (and), or ~ (not), each condition must be grouped in parentheses, because Python would otherwise evaluate the comparison operators in an unintended order: `orders[(orders["city"] == "Lagos") & (orders["delivery_time_minutes"] > 25)]` needs those parentheses around each comparison to work correctly.
A boolean filter is really just a same-length True/False column you compute first, then hand to [] to keep only the rows marked True -- one condition, or several grouped in parentheses.

A single rename() call can rename columns and index labels together by passing both the columns and index arguments at once; any label not included in the mapping is left unchanged: `orders.rename(columns={"city": "destination_city"}, index={0: "first_order"})` relabels one column and one row label in a single call, leaving every other label as it was.

The astype() method explicitly converts a column's (or Series') values from one dtype to another, returning a copy by default, and it raises an exception if the requested conversion is invalid: `orders["distance_km"] = orders["distance_km"].astype(float)` converts the text values to actual floats -- but if one row instead held "unknown", astype would raise an exception rather than silently guessing.

astype() can convert a single column, a subset of a DataFrame's columns at once, or specific columns to specific dtypes by passing a dict mapping column names to target dtypes: `orders.astype({"distance_km": float, "order_id": str})` converts two columns to two different target types in one call.
astype() is the tool for "this column's dtype is wrong for what I need to do with it" -- but it only succeeds if every value can actually be reinterpreted as the target type.

Once a column has a datetime dtype, its .dt accessor exposes date/time component properties, such as year, month, and day, for each value: `orders["pickup_month"] = orders["pickup_date"].dt.month` pulls just the month number out of every pickup date at once.

By default, drop_duplicates() keeps the first occurrence of each duplicate set and drops the rest; passing keep='last' keeps the last occurrence instead, and keep=False drops every row that is part of a duplicate set: `orders.drop_duplicates(subset=["order_id"], keep="last")` would keep order #1042's second logged row instead of its first.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose a handful of orders never got a delivery_time_minutes recorded -- those cells are just blank.
isna() (and its complement notna()) detects which values in a Series or DataFrame are missing: `orders["delivery_time_minutes"].isna()` returns True for every order missing that value.

dropna() removes rows that contain missing values; passing a subset of column labels restricts which columns are checked when deciding whether a row counts as having a missing value: `orders.dropna(subset=["delivery_time_minutes"])` removes only the orders missing that one column, ignoring gaps elsewhere.

fillna() replaces missing (NA) values with a specified value, such as a scalar (for example, replacing every missing value in a column with 0): `orders["delivery_time_minutes"].fillna(orders["delivery_time_minutes"].median())` replaces each missing delivery time with the column's median value instead of dropping the order entirely.

Handling missing data means detecting it first, then deciding what to do about it -- for example, dropping the order if a missing delivery time makes that row unusable for the analysis at hand, or filling it with the column's median if a reasonable substitute exists instead.

pd.concat() concatenates multiple Series or DataFrame objects along an axis: `pd.concat([jan_orders, feb_orders, mar_orders])`.

By default, pd.concat() stacks the given DataFrames row-wise, appending each one's rows below the previous, producing one combined DataFrame when they share the same columns -- so the result above has every January row, then every February row, then every March row, one after another.

pd.concat() takes an axis parameter: by default (no axis argument), it stacks the objects row-wise, while axis=1 places them side by side as columns: `pd.concat([orders_basic_info, orders_extra_columns], axis=1)` would instead line the two tables up next to each other, column by column.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose orders live in one DataFrame and driver details live in another, linked by a shared driver_id column.
merge() combines two DataFrames by matching values in a shared key column, which can be specified with the on parameter: `orders.merge(drivers, on="driver_id")`.

The how parameter to merge() controls which keys are kept in the result; how='inner' (the default) keeps only the key values present in both DataFrames -- so a driver_id that appears in orders but not in drivers wouldn't survive an inner merge, and vice versa.

If a key value does not appear in one of the two DataFrames being merged, the corresponding values contributed by that DataFrame in the joined result are NA -- which is what happens once a join type other than the default inner merge is used, and unmatched keys are allowed to stay in the result.

The how parameter also accepts 'left' (keep all keys from the left DataFrame only), 'right' (keep all keys from the right DataFrame only), and 'outer' (keep the union of keys from both DataFrames): `orders.merge(drivers, on="driver_id", how="left")` keeps every order, filling in NA for driver details on any driver_id merge can't find in the drivers table.
merge() matches rows on a shared key; setting the how parameter decides whether unmatched rows on either side get dropped or kept with NA gaps.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose you want the average delivery time per city, not for the whole batch of orders at once.

Group by refers to a process involving one or more of the following steps: splitting the data into groups based on some criteria, applying a function to each group independently, and combining the results into a data structure -- split every order into its city's group, apply "average" within each group, then combine the per-city averages into one result.
An aggregation is a groupby operation that reduces each group to a single summary value per column, such as computing the sum of a column within each group.

In practice, you call df.groupby(key) and then an aggregation method such as .sum() or .mean() on the DataFrame or a selected column, or .agg([...]) to compute several aggregations at once; by default the group keys become the index of the result: `orders.groupby("city")["delivery_time_minutes"].mean()` returns one average delivery time per city, with the city names as the index; `orders.groupby("city")["delivery_time_minutes"].agg(["mean", "sum"])` computes both the average and the total in one call.
Split, apply, combine is the whole idea -- groupby just gives you one call that does all three steps for whatever key and aggregation you choose.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose a wide summary table has one row per city and separate columns "jan_deliveries", "feb_deliveries", "mar_deliveries" -- and you need one row per city-month combination instead.

melt() reshapes a DataFrame from wide to long format: the columns listed as id_vars stay as identifier columns, while all other columns are unpivoted into two columns, one holding the original column names and one holding their values: `city_deliveries.melt(id_vars=["city"])` keeps "city" as an identifier and turns "jan_deliveries", "feb_deliveries", and "mar_deliveries" into two new columns -- one holding those original column names, the other holding each of their counts.

The default 'variable' and 'value' column names produced by melt() can be renamed using its var_name and value_name parameters: `city_deliveries.melt(id_vars=["city"], var_name="month", value_name="deliveries")` gives those two new columns clearer names.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the long table that melt produced earlier is saved as long_deliveries, with one row per city-month and the columns city, month, and deliveries -- and it needs to go back to a wide table: cities as rows, months as columns.

pivot_table() reshapes data by turning the distinct values of one column into new columns, and unlike plain pivot(), it can handle duplicate index/column combinations by aggregating the numeric values.

pivot_table() takes index, columns, and values arguments: index sets the rows of the output table, columns sets the new columns, and values selects which column(s) to aggregate into the table: `long_deliveries.pivot_table(index="city", columns="month", values="deliveries")` puts each city on its own row, each month as its own column, and the delivery counts as the values filling the grid.

pivot_table() combines rows that share the same index/column values using aggfunc, which defaults to 'mean'; passing aggfunc='sum' (or another function) changes how those values are combined -- so if a city had two rows for the same month, the default call above would average them instead of erroring, and adding aggfunc="sum" would total them instead.
pivot_table spreads long data wider by turning one column's values into new column headers, aggregating whenever more than one row lands in the same cell.

to_csv()'s index argument controls whether the row (index) labels are written to the file; it defaults to True, and passing index=False omits them: `orders.to_csv("cleaned_orders.csv", index=False)` writes the same file without an extra index column.

teaching_blocks.content: Now that you've worked with a single delivery-orders table in pandas, picture the same business run out of a real database instead of one spreadsheet: a customers table, an orders table, a products table, each living on its own. A relational database is built out of exactly this kind of piece.

A relation -- what SQL calls a table -- holds data where each row (also called a record or tuple) represents one group of related data values, and its columns are also called fields or attributes. So the customers table's rows are individual customers, and its columns (customer_id, name, city) are the attributes recorded about every customer. A database is composed of multiple tables like this, each holding its own kind of data -- customers, orders and products each get their own table rather than being crammed together.

A few properties keep a table well-formed. It has a name distinct from every other table in the database -- 'customers' is not also used for anything else -- and it contains no duplicate rows; the order its rows and columns happen to be listed in is not meaningful. On top of that, each table should contain information about one kind of thing only, such as the Customer or the Order, rather than mixing unrelated things into one table -- which is exactly why a customer's details and an order's details live in two separate tables instead of one merged one.

Reading a relational database, then, starts with the same question every time: which table am I looking at, what one kind of thing does each of its rows represent, and what does each column tell me about that thing. That question is what the SELECT statement you write next will answer.

teaching_blocks.content: You know the customers table has columns customer_id, name and city. To actually pull that data out of the database, you write a SELECT statement.

The SELECT list -- everything between the keywords SELECT and FROM -- specifies the expressions that form the output rows of the statement, and the FROM clause derives the table (or tables) the query reads from. So SELECT name, city FROM customers reads the customers table and returns just those two columns, for every row.

You can also rename an output column by writing AS output_name after its expression in the SELECT list -- AS can be left out if the name you want doesn't collide with a keyword. SELECT name AS customer_name, city FROM customers returns the same data, but the first column is now labeled customer_name in the result instead of name.

Writing * in the SELECT list is shorthand for all columns of the selected rows, so SELECT * FROM customers returns every column of every customer row without listing them one by one; table_name.* narrows that to just one table's columns when a query reads from more than one table.
SELECT ... FROM is the shape every query in this path builds on: FROM says which table to read, and the SELECT list says which columns -- renamed or not -- come back out.

teaching_blocks.content: Typing out orders or customers in full every time gets tedious, especially once a query starts referring to a table's columns repeatedly. SQL lets you give a table a short temporary name for the query instead.

A table alias is a temporary name given to a table reference, written FROM table_reference AS alias, with AS optional -- FROM orders AS o gives the orders table the short name o for the rest of that query. Once assigned, the table must be referred to by its alias, not its original name, for the remainder of the query -- writing FROM orders AS o and then referencing orders again later would be an error.

A column can be aliased the same way, by writing AS output_name after the column's expression in the SELECT list, exactly as you already saw with SELECT. A column can also be referenced as correlation.columnname, where correlation is a table name or an alias defined in the FROM clause -- so with orders aliased to o, you can write o.customer_id instead of orders.customer_id. The correlation name and dot can be left off entirely when the column name is unique across every table used in the query.

On a single table like SELECT o.order_id, o.delivery_time_minutes FROM orders AS o, qualifying a column this way is optional. The alias starts to matter once a query reads from more than one table at a time and two of those tables happen to share a column name -- qualifying which table's copy you mean is what keeps the query unambiguous.
Whether it's naming a table or a column, an alias is the same idea: a temporary rename that exists only for the current query, chosen to make the query shorter or its columns clearer to read.

teaching_blocks.content: SELECT DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result, keeping one row from each group of duplicates. SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers returns each city that appears in the customers table exactly once, no matter how many customers share it.

SELECT ALL is the default behavior when DISTINCT is not written -- it keeps every row, duplicates included. So SELECT city FROM customers (no DISTINCT) would list Lagos once per customer who lives there, while SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers lists Lagos only once.

teaching_blocks.content: SELECT * FROM orders returns every order. To ask a real question -- 'which orders took a long time to deliver?' -- you need to narrow that down to just the matching rows.

WHERE takes a search condition that evaluates to a boolean value for each row; a row is kept in the output only if the condition is true, and discarded otherwise. SELECT order_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 40 keeps only the orders whose delivery time exceeds 40 minutes.

The comparison operators <, >, <=, >=, =, and <> compare two values of the same or a compatible type and produce a boolean result: = tests for equal and <> tests for not equal (!= is an alias for <>). WHERE customer_id = 2 keeps only orders placed by customer 2; WHERE delivery_time_minutes <> 20 keeps the orders whose recorded delivery time is something other than 20 minutes.
WHERE is evaluated per row: for each row it asks 'is this condition true for this row?' and keeps the rows where the answer is yes.
