teaching_blocks.content: The delivery company wants to know whether a redesigned checkout button on its ordering app gets more people to complete an order. Rather than guess, it runs a controlled test on real users.

Studies where researchers assign treatments to cases are called experiments; when the assignment includes randomization, it is called a randomized experiment. Researchers randomly assign cases to a control group and a treatment group so that differences between the groups that cannot otherwise be controlled are evened out.

A/B testing works by showing two variants of a page or experience to users at random: the original (control, or A) and a modified version (variation, or B); engagement with each version is measured and then compared against the baseline, the control. For the checkout button, the existing button is the control (A), the redesigned button is the treatment (B), users are randomly shown one or the other, and the metric compared is the share of each group that completes an order.
Every A/B test has these parts: a control group, a treatment group, and the measure being compared between them. The treatment group's result is then compared against the control, the baseline.

video_need.reason: Randomly splitting one population of users into two groups that each experience something different is a spatial/process relationship -- a diagram showing users being randomly routed into a control arm and a treatment arm makes the structure clearer than describing the split in words.

teaching_blocks.content: Once the checkout-button test has run, the raw numbers -- say, a 20% completion rate for the control button and a 22% completion rate for the redesigned one -- need to be turned into a comparison that's easy to talk about.

Relative improvement (lift) is the percentage difference in the variation's conversion rate over the baseline (control) conversion rate; for example, a 10% relative improvement over a 25% baseline conversion rate means the variation's conversion rate is 27.5%. Relative improvement describes the variation's change as a percentage of the baseline's rate.

Applying that to the checkout test: a treatment rate of 22% over a control rate of 20% is a 2-percentage-point difference, which as a percentage of the 20% baseline is a 10% lift -- the same 10%-relative-improvement structure as the textbook example, just with the checkout numbers.

Analyzing an A/B test's results means determining whether the variation had a positive, negative, or neutral effect compared with the baseline (control). Lift puts the observed difference into one figure: a positive lift means the variation's rate came out above the control's in this test, and a negative lift means it came out below.

video_need.reason: Lift is a percentage-change calculation on two numbers that are already known; the worked example fully shows how to compute and read it, with no mechanism, UI, or changing state to demonstrate.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose two versions of the checkout-button test both come back showing the same 10% lift -- but one ran with 50 users in each group and the other ran with 5,000 users in each group. Should you trust them equally?

A bigger sample tends to provide a more precise point estimate than a smaller sample. The more cases researchers observe, the more accurately they can estimate the effect of the explanatory variable (here, which button a user saw) on the response (whether they completed an order); in a single study, this is done by collecting a sufficiently large sample.

So the 5,000-user version of the checkout test tends to provide a more precise estimate of the button's effect than the 50-user version, even though both happened to show the same 10% lift -- the larger test observed far more cases, so it can estimate the button's effect on completed orders more accurately.

video_need.reason: The idea that small-sample estimates scatter more widely around the true effect than large-sample ones is a spread that's easier to picture with a diagram of estimates clustering tightly for the large sample and spreading widely for the small one than to hold in mind from a description alone.

teaching_blocks.content: The checkout test showed a 10% lift for the redesigned button. Before recommending it company-wide, you need language for how sure that result actually is.

The null hypothesis (H0) often represents a skeptical position or a perspective of "no difference", and the alternative hypothesis (HA) represents an alternative claim under consideration. For the checkout test, H0 would be that the redesigned button makes no real difference to completion rate, and HA would be that it does.

The p-value is the probability of observing data at least as favorable to the alternative hypothesis as our current data set, if the null hypothesis were true -- it quantifies the strength of evidence against the null hypothesis. Statistical significance measures how unusual a result would be if there were actually no difference between the variation and the baseline and the discrepancy were due to chance alone.

A confidence interval is a range of plausible values likely to contain the population parameter (the true value you are trying to estimate); if many samples were taken and a 95% interval built from each one, about 95% of those intervals would contain it.

Describing a confidence interval as capturing the population parameter with a certain probability is a common error; while it may be useful to think of it that way, the confidence level only quantifies how plausible it is that the parameter is in the given interval. So it's not quite right to say "there's a 95% chance the true completion-rate difference is in this interval" -- the 95% describes how the method behaves across many samples, not the probability attached to this one interval.

Not every confidence interval captures the true value, even when the method is followed correctly: in an illustrative set of twenty-five 95% confidence intervals built from different samples (around p = 0.88), only one failed to contain the population proportion -- showing that a small fraction of intervals will miss it. The same is true of any single confidence interval you compute for a result like the checkout test.

When the sample size becomes large, even a very small, practically unimportant difference can be detected and called statistically significant; such a difference is statistically significant but not practically significant. A large enough checkout test could detect a tiny, practically unimportant lift and call it statistically significant -- significance tells you how unusual the result would be if there were truly no difference, not that the lift is big enough to matter.

video_need.reason: Hypotheses, p-values, and confidence intervals are all defined in terms of what would happen across many repeated samples -- an animation showing repeated samples each producing their own interval, most catching the true value and a few missing it, makes that repeated-sampling idea concrete in a way that a single static definition can't.

teaching_blocks.content: Getting a p-value or confidence interval isn't the end of the job -- someone still has to decide what to do about the checkout button.

As before, H0 often represents a skeptical perspective or a claim to be tested, and HA an alternative claim under consideration; the value being compared to the parameter in this setup is called the null value.

Consider two textbook examples, each testing whether a proportion equals a null value of 0.333. In one, because the null value (p0 = 0.333) fell within the confidence interval computed from the sample, that value was not implausible, so the data did not provide sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis. In a second, the null value (p0 = 0.333) was not in the 95% confidence interval, so the null hypothesis was rejected: the data provided statistically significant evidence that the proportion differed from 0.333, and because the entire interval was below 0.333, it was concluded to be lower.

While the first example failed to reject the null hypothesis, that does not necessarily mean the null hypothesis is true; perhaps there was an actual difference, but it could not be detected with the relatively small sample of 50. Failing to reject the null hypothesis is not equivalent to accepting the null hypothesis as true; it only means there was not strong enough evidence for the alternative.

Analyzing a test's results means saying whether the variation had a positive, negative, or neutral effect versus the baseline (control). For the checkout test, that means stating plainly whether the redesigned button did better, worse, or about the same as the original -- not just reporting a p-value and stopping. If the checkout test's summary showed its null value inside the confidence interval, the conclusion would be that the data did not provide sufficient evidence of a difference -- not that the new button makes no difference.

When the sample size becomes large, even a very small, practically unimportant difference can be detected and called statistically significant; for example, an online experiment might find that placing additional ads on a movie review website statistically significantly increases viewership of a TV show by 0.001%, but this increase might not have any practical value. A business conclusion has to weigh that: a statistically significant lift on the checkout button might still be too small to have any practical value, so look at the size of the lift, not just whether it was detected.

video_need.reason: The two contrasting outcomes -- a null value sitting inside a confidence interval versus falling outside it -- are easier to place and compare with a number-line diagram showing the interval and where the null value lands than to hold in mind from the worked numbers alone.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose you have this week's delivery times -- 18, 22, 26, 19, 30 minutes -- and you want to see them as a graph instead of a list of numbers. Matplotlib is the library that draws that graph, but it draws onto two different kinds of object, not just "a plot". Matplotlib graphs data on Figures, and each Figure can contain one or more Axes, which is the area where data is actually plotted.

The Figure is the overall canvas: the whole window or image you eventually display or save. An Axes is one plotting area that lives inside that Figure -- the rectangle with its own x- and y-axis where lines, bars, or points are actually drawn. A single Figure can hold more than one Axes, but even the simplest plot needs at least one.

After `import matplotlib.pyplot as plt`, `fig, ax = plt.subplots()` creates a Figure and one Axes together, giving explicit variables for both objects: `fig` refers to the whole canvas, and `ax` refers to the one plotting area inside it.

Plotting calls such as `ax.plot(x, y)` draw onto that specific Axes object. `fig, ax = plt.subplots()` followed by `ax.plot([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [18, 22, 26, 19, 30])` draws the week's delivery times as a line onto `ax`. `fig` itself doesn't receive any plotted data directly -- it just holds the Axes that does.

With `plt.subplots()`, you get a Figure and an Axes first, then call a plotting method on the Axes, not the Figure. Keeping the two straight -- Figure is the canvas, Axes is where the data goes -- makes plotting calls like `ax.plot()` easier to read.

video_need.reason: The Figure-as-canvas / Axes-as-plotting-area relationship is a spatial container relationship that is easier to picture when it is highlighted on screen and watched being created and drawn onto, though the text's canvas framing and the worked fig/ax example already make the idea workable from text alone.

teaching_notes: Establish the Figure/Axes container relationship clearly before any other viz concept -- everything in this tile builds on fig, ax = plt.subplots().
Don't introduce figsize or tight_layout here -- that's viz.figure_size_layout next.

teaching_blocks.content: `plt.subplots(figsize=(width, height))` sets the figure's dimensions. `figsize` is a (width, height) tuple, measured in inches, and its default is `rcParams['figure.figsize']`, which itself defaults to `[6.4, 4.8]`. `fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))` makes a wider-than-default figure, 8 inches by 4 inches, and `fig.tight_layout()` then adjusts the spacing to fit.

`tight_layout()` automatically adjusts subplot parameters so the subplot(s) fit into the figure area; it works by checking the extents of tick labels, axis labels, and titles. It can be called as `plt.tight_layout()` or `fig.tight_layout()`.

video_need.reason: figsize and tight_layout are two keyword-level settings with no moving parts to demonstrate; a short paragraph and the two code lines are enough.

teaching_blocks.content: You have already seen `ax.plot(x, y)` draw onto an Axes you created with `plt.subplots()`. pyplot also has its own `plot()` function, called directly as `plt.plot()`, and it accepts data in two different forms.

`plt.plot(y)` called with a single array argument treats it as the y-values and automatically generates the x-values starting from 0. Given just the delivery times `[18, 22, 26, 19, 30]`, `plt.plot([18, 22, 26, 19, 30])` plots those five values against the automatic x-positions 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.

`plt.plot(x, y)` called with two array arguments plots the y-values against the given x-values instead. `plt.plot([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [18, 22, 26, 19, 30])` plots the same five delivery times, but now against the day numbers 1 through 5 you supplied, rather than the automatic 0-based positions.
Both forms call the same function and produce a similar-looking line; the only difference is whether you hand `plot()` an explicit x-axis or let it fill one in for you starting at 0.

video_need.reason: Seeing the one-array call auto-number its x-axis from 0, side by side with the two-array call using the supplied x-values, makes the difference between the two forms concrete in a way the text's description approximates.

Here, teach plt.plot()'s two argument forms generically, without the 'trend' framing -- that framing is introduced next.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose you want to compare average delivery time across three cities -- Lagos, Abuja, and Kano -- rather than look at individual deliveries. A bar chart is a common chart type for graphing categorical data or data sorted into groups, which fits this comparison exactly.

`plt.bar(x, height)` (or `ax.bar(x, height)`) makes a bar plot with bars positioned at the given x coordinates and given heights, with the baseline defaulting to 0. Categorical variables such as names can be passed directly as the x argument, rather than only numeric x-positions: `city_avg = orders.groupby("city")["delivery_time_minutes"].mean()` stores one average per city, with the city names as its index, and `plt.bar(city_avg.index, city_avg)` plots those three city names directly as the bars' x-positions, with each city's average as its bar height.

Bar charts are easy to interpret because the eye is good at comparing lengths when the objects being compared are aligned to a common baseline -- here, every bar starts at 0, so the bar for Kano simply looks taller than Lagos's because its average delivery time is higher.

It can seem harmless to start the bars at some value other than 0 -- say at 20 minutes, to make small differences between cities stand out. That distorts the comparison. A bar chart is easy to read because the eye compares bar lengths from a common baseline, so the lengths themselves have to stay true to the values. If Kano averages 30 minutes and Lagos 25, bars that start at 20 are 10 and 5 units tall: Kano's bar looks twice as long as Lagos's even though its average is only 5 minutes higher. Keep the baseline at 0.

video_need.reason: Why the shared zero baseline matters is a before/after comparison -- the same three city averages rendered with a shared baseline versus a shifted one look like they tell different stories, which is far more convincing seen than described.

teaching_notes: Build on pandas.groupby_aggregation's own orders/city/delivery_time_minutes example so the dataset is familiar.

teaching_blocks.content: A bar chart compares categories, but delivery times themselves are a numeric variable, and you might instead want to see how those times are distributed -- how many deliveries were fast, how many were slow.

`plt.hist(x, bins=...)` uses `numpy.histogram` to bin the data in `x`, count the number of values in each bin, and draw the result as bars. `plt.hist(orders["delivery_time_minutes"])` bins every delivery's time and shows how many deliveries fall in each time range.

The `bins` parameter defaults to `rcParams['hist.bins']`, which defaults to 10; passing an integer sets that many equal-width bins, passing a sequence sets explicit bin edges, and passing a string such as `'auto'` selects a binning strategy. `plt.hist(orders["delivery_time_minutes"], bins=5)` groups the data into 5 equal-width bins instead of the default 10. Each bar's height shows how many deliveries fall into that bin, so a taller bar means more deliveries took that range of time.

video_need.reason: How the same delivery-time data reshapes as the bin count changes is a changing-state effect that is clearer watched live -- going from 5 bins to 10 to 'auto' on screen shows directly how bin choice can hide or reveal structure in a way a static description can only assert.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose you have this week's average Lagos delivery time for each of 5 days and want to see whether it is getting better or worse. Line graphs are best when you want to show how the value of something changes over time, or compare how several things change over time relative to each other.
A line graph plots the measured points and then draws a line that connects those points, making it easier to see how the values rose, fell, or stayed the same over time.

`plt.plot(x, y)` plots the y-values against the given x-values. `plt.plot([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [21, 23, 19, 25, 20])` plots 5 days of average Lagos delivery times, with the connecting line making the day-to-day rise and fall visible at a glance in a way the five numbers alone would not be.

video_need.reason: Watching the line get drawn point by point reinforces how the connecting line, not just the points, is what makes a rise or fall readable, though the text's description and the day-by-day example largely cover this.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose you want to see whether delivery distance and delivery time move together across your orders, rather than compare categories or track a trend over time. A scatterplot shows the relationship between two numerical variables plotted simultaneously along the horizontal and vertical axis, and is useful for focusing on the relationship between two series.

`plt.scatter(x, y)` (or `ax.scatter(x, y)`) makes a scatter plot of the y-values against the x-values, one point per (x, y) pair. `plt.scatter(orders["distance_km"], orders["delivery_time_minutes"])` plots one point per order, with each point's position showing that order's distance and delivery time together.

video_need.reason: Seeing the point cloud appear order by order helps connect 'one point per row' to the resulting shape, though the text's definition and the distance/delivery-time example already convey the idea.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose you want to compare the full spread of delivery times across Lagos, Abuja, and Kano -- not just their averages, but how spread out and how extreme each city's times get. Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side.

`plt.boxplot(x)` (or `ax.boxplot(x)`) draws a box plot from the data in `x`; it accepts array-like data and can draw one or more boxes. The box extends from the first quartile (Q1) to the third quartile (Q3) of the data, with a line at the median. The whiskers extend from the box to the farthest data point lying within 1.5x the interquartile range (IQR) from the box; points past the end of the whiskers are flier points (outliers). For example, if Lagos's box runs from Q1 = 20 minutes to Q3 = 30 minutes, the interquartile range (IQR) is the length of the box: 30 - 20 = 10 minutes. The whiskers can then reach at most 1.5 x 10 = 15 minutes beyond the box -- no lower than 5 minutes and no higher than 45 minutes -- so a 50-minute Lagos delivery would be drawn as a separate flier point.

Passing a sequence of 1D arrays as `x` draws one box for each array in the sequence; `tick_labels=[...]` labels each boxplot's tick accordingly instead of leaving it as a numeric value. `lagos_times = orders.loc[orders["city"] == "Lagos", "delivery_time_minutes"]` pulls out just the Lagos delivery times by boolean filtering, and `abuja_times`/`kano_times` are built the same way for the other two cities. `plt.boxplot([lagos_times, abuja_times, kano_times], tick_labels=["Lagos", "Abuja", "Kano"])` then draws three boxes side by side, one per city, each labeled with its city name instead of 1, 2, 3.

video_need.reason: The box/whisker anatomy -- which edge is Q1 versus Q3, where the median line sits, what counts as a whisker versus a flier point -- is a labeled-diagram concept that is far clearer pointed-to on an annotated drawing than described purely in words.

teaching_blocks.content: Titles, axis labels, and legends are the text that tells a reader what a plot shows. Matplotlib gives two parallel ways to add them, depending on whether you are working with an Axes object or the pyplot interface directly.

`ax.set_xlabel('...')` and `ax.set_ylabel('...')` set the x-axis and y-axis labels, and `ax.set_title('...')` sets the Axes title. `ax.set_xlabel("Day")`, `ax.set_ylabel("Average delivery time (minutes)")`, and `ax.set_title("Average delivery time by day")` label the Lagos trend line from before.

Passing `label='...'` to a plotting call (e.g. `ax.plot(data, label='data1')`) and then calling `ax.legend()` displays a legend identifying each labeled series. `days = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]` and `lagos_avg = [21, 23, 19, 25, 20]` are the same 5 days of Lagos averages from before, so `ax.plot(days, lagos_avg, label="Lagos")` followed by `ax.legend()` shows a legend identifying the Lagos line, which matters once a second city's line is added to the same Axes.

In the pyplot interface, `plt.xlabel()`, `plt.ylabel()`, and `plt.title()` set the same label/title elements on the current Axes -- the pyplot equivalents of `ax.set_xlabel()`, `ax.set_ylabel()`, and `ax.set_title()`.

teaching_blocks.content: With five chart types available, the question during your own exploration is which one actually answers the question you're asking of the data.

A bar chart is used for graphing categorical data and comparing values across categories -- average delivery time per city, for instance. `plt.hist()` bins a numeric variable, counts values per bin, and draws the distribution as bars -- useful for how delivery times themselves are spread out. Line graphs are best when you want to show how a value changes over time, or compare how several things change over time relative to each other -- average delivery time across the days of the week. A scatterplot shows the relationship between two numerical variables plotted along the horizontal and vertical axis -- whether distance and delivery time move together. Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side -- the full spread of delivery times across several cities at once, not just their averages.

Picking a chart type during exploration comes down to naming what you're actually asking: a category comparison, a single variable's spread, a trend over time, a relationship between two variables, or a spread comparison across several groups.

teaching_blocks.content: Most plotting calls so far have needed you to pull a column or an array out of `orders` yourself before plotting it. Seaborn's plotting functions operate on dataframes and arrays containing whole datasets, taking only the names of the variables and their roles in the plot (for example `data=`, `x=`, `y=`) rather than requiring the caller to extract each array.

`seaborn.barplot(data=..., x=..., y=...)` visualizes an aggregate statistical estimate for each category as a bar; its default estimator is the mean, and it draws an error bar (uncertainty indicator) around each bar by default. teaching_blocks.content: During your own exploration, you might have built a bar chart, a line plot, and a box plot of the delivery data. Presenting to the operations manager, the question changes: which one actually makes the Lagos point, for this audience?

A bar chart is used for graphing categorical data and comparing values across categories -- showing average delivery time side by side across Lagos, Abuja, and Kano. Line graphs are best when you want to show how the value of something changes over time, or compare how several things change over time relative to each other -- showing Lagos delivery time rising week over week. Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side -- but a boxplot may be unfamiliar to many people and could introduce a learning curve, so choosing a different display altogether may avoid confusion for audiences who do not know this chart type or how to read it; for a manager who hasn't seen a box plot before, the bar chart or line plot can often make the point more directly.

A pie chart expresses a part-to-whole relationship in the data, and is best used either for a general sense of how parts relate to the whole, or to highlight that one segment is notably larger or smaller than the others; the pie must depict a meaningful whole (values that sum to 100%). If the point is "Lagos accounts for most of our total delivery volume," a pie chart of each city's share of total orders fits that part-to-whole framing in a way a bar chart of averages would not.

A scatterplot is often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it, though it can still be designed to convey findings to an audience -- useful to keep in mind if the distance/delivery-time relationship ever needs to go in front of the manager directly, rather than staying an exploratory chart.

It can look like comparing pie slices is just as easy as comparing bar lengths, since both show a value at a glance -- but it is not. A bar chart's aligned, common baseline makes length differences easy to judge; two pie slices of similar size are harder to rank correctly by eye.

teaching_blocks.content: The first executable step of the workflow is retrieving last quarter's orders with SQL.

A single SELECT statement's syntax allows a FROM clause, a WHERE clause, and a GROUP BY clause to appear together in the same query. In the capstone, that means the orders query can filter down to last quarter's rows and group the result by zone in one statement, rather than as separate steps.

A join, such as an INNER JOIN, can be included in that same SELECT statement's FROM clause to combine matching rows from more than one table before the query's WHERE filtering or GROUP BY grouping is applied. In the capstone, that means the orders and drivers tables can be joined in the same FROM clause, before the WHERE and GROUP BY narrow and group the combined rows.

Combined, the capstone's retrieval query looks like: SELECT o.zone, AVG(o.delivery_time) FROM orders o INNER JOIN drivers d ON o.driver_id = d.driver_id WHERE o.order_date >= '2026-04-01' AND o.order_date < '2026-07-01' GROUP BY o.zone; -- the join combines each order with its matching driver row first, the WHERE clause then narrows the rows to last quarter (April 1 to June 30), and the GROUP BY groups what's left by zone, so AVG gives one average delivery time per zone.
None of this is new SQL syntax -- it's the same SELECT, FROM, WHERE, JOIN, and GROUP BY already learned, aimed at the capstone's own question.

A PivotTable is built by selecting the data range and inserting a PivotTable, then adding fields to it: non-numeric fields default to Rows, date/time fields to Columns, and numeric fields to Values, and fields can be dragged between these areas to rearrange the summary. In the capstone, that means the delivery sheet's zone and shift fields default into Rows while delivery_time defaults into Values, ready to be rearranged into a more useful layout.

COUNTIFS(criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2]...) applies criteria across one or more ranges and counts the cells for which all the criteria are met. In the capstone, that means counting how many deliveries in a specific zone exceeded a time threshold, using the zone and the time as the two criteria.

For the capstone's delivery sheet, where each row pairs an order's zone and delivery_time with its driver's shift from the roster: selecting the data range, inserting a PivotTable and adding those fields puts zone and shift -- both non-numeric -- in Rows by default, and delivery_time, which is numeric, in Values. Dragging shift from Rows to Columns rearranges the summary into a zone-by-shift grid, and changing the Values field's summary function to Average makes each cell an average delivery time. Separately, COUNTIFS(zone_range, "Ikeja", delivery_time_range, ">45") counts how many Ikeja deliveries in the sheet took more than 45 minutes, since both criteria -- the zone and the time threshold -- must be met at once.
The PivotTable and COUNTIFS skills already learned are now run on this project's own roster and delivery data instead of a practice file.

teaching_blocks.content: Once orders and roster are both retrieved, pandas is where they get cleaned and combined for the actual analysis.

isna() detects which values in a DataFrame are missing, and dropna() removes rows with missing values or fillna() replaces them with a specified value. In the capstone, that means flagging which of the retrieved orders are missing a delivery_time before deciding whether to drop or fill those rows.

A groupby operation splits data into groups based on some criteria, applies a function independently to each group, and combines the results back into a single structure; an aggregation is a groupby operation that reduces each group to one summary value per column. In the capstone, that means splitting the cleaned orders by zone and reducing each zone's delivery times to one summary number.

On the capstone's retrieved orders, orders['delivery_time'].isna() flags rows with no delivery time recorded; those rows get removed with dropna() (or, where a default makes sense, filled with fillna()). Then orders.groupby('zone')['delivery_time'].mean() splits the cleaned orders by zone, computes the mean delivery time independently within each zone, and combines the per-zone results into one summary -- an aggregation, since each zone group is reduced to a single number.
The same isna()/dropna()/fillna() and groupby skills already learned are now run on the capstone's own retrieved data instead of a practice dataset.

teaching_blocks.content: The capstone's data spans two tables -- Orders and Drivers -- so before deeper analysis relies on both together, they need to be modeled as related tables.

A primary key uniquely identifies each row of a table; a foreign key's values must match values appearing in some row of the table it references. In the capstone, that means the Drivers table needs a column that uniquely identifies each driver, and the Orders table needs a column whose values must match one of those driver identifiers.

In a one-to-many relationship, one row on the 'one' side relates to many rows on the 'many' side (for example, one department has many employees); in the Customer/Order example, the foreign key CustID is placed in the Order table and must match a valid CustID in the Customer table. In the capstone, that means one driver can appear in many orders, the same one-to-many pattern as one customer having many orders.

Mapped onto the capstone: Drivers has driver_id as its primary key, uniquely identifying each driver row. Orders has its own primary key, order_id, plus a driver_id column that is a foreign key -- its values must match a driver_id that already exists in Drivers. Since one driver delivers many orders, this is a one-to-many relationship: one row on the Drivers ('one') side relates to many rows on the Orders ('many') side, the same pattern as CustID sitting in the Order table and matching a valid CustID in the Customer table.
Getting the primary key/foreign key pairing right connects the two tables correctly before any join or aggregation across them can be trusted.

teaching_blocks.content: With cleaned, modeled data, the business question needs actual numbers: how late are deliveries, by zone?

describe() computes a variety of summary statistics about a Series or the columns of a DataFrame. In the capstone, that means running describe() on a zone's delivery_time column to get that summary in one call.

The mean is more strongly affected by extreme observations than the median, which is more robust to them; so when the goal is to understand a typical individual value in a skewed dataset, the median can be more useful. In the capstone, that means checking whether a handful of unusually long deliveries are skewing a zone's average before trusting it as typical.

Running describe() on one zone's delivery_time column returns a mean of 52 minutes, with the median (the middle quartile in describe()'s output) at 38 minutes. But a handful of deliveries in that zone took over three hours -- a stalled vehicle, a wrong address -- and the mean is pulled up by those extreme observations, while the median, more robust to them, stays at 38 minutes. The capstone's business question is which zones are missing the delivery-time target and by how much, which calls for judging a typical delivery against that target rather than one skewed by a few rare extremes, so the median is the more useful number here.
describe() gives the full summary; deciding whether the mean or the median actually answers the business question depends on whether extreme values are skewing that particular column.

teaching_blocks.content: The findings now need a visualization set a stakeholder can look at, not just numbers in a table.

fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2) creates one Figure containing a 2x2 grid of Axes, so several charts can share one figure. In the capstone, that means four related delivery charts can share one figure instead of as four separate figures.

plt.subplot(131), plt.subplot(132), and plt.subplot(133) can each hold a different chart side by side in one figure, and plt.suptitle() adds one title over the whole figure. In the capstone, that means three of the delivery charts can instead sit side by side under one shared title.

For the capstone, fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2) lays out four related charts -- delivery time by zone, delivery time by shift, order count by zone, and the distribution of delivery times -- in one 2x2 figure. Alternatively, plt.subplot(131), plt.subplot(132), plt.subplot(133) place three of those charts side by side in a single row, and plt.suptitle('Delivery Performance -- Last Quarter') puts one title over all three so they read as one visualization set.
Either layout turns several separate charts into one coherent figure the stakeholder summary can point to as a set.

teaching_blocks.content: With the plan, retrieval, cleaning, modeling, statistics, and visualization steps all defined, what's left is carrying the whole thing out yourself, end to end, without being walked through each step again.

During the design phase, the commission is converted into an analytical plan, with some iteration expected as the solution is developed. For the capstone, the workflow outline from earlier becomes that analytical plan, and it's normal to adjust it once the SQL, spreadsheet, and pandas work actually starts.

During the analysis phase, the planned analysis is carried out while progress and relevance are monitored, and appropriate records of the analysis conducted, changes, decisions, and assumptions made are maintained. So as the capstone's query, cleaning, modeling, statistics, and figures get built, a short record of what was decided -- for example, how missing delivery times were handled -- is kept alongside a check that the results still answer the original zone-delay question.
Independent execution is running the whole plan yourself, adjusting it as needed, and keeping a record of the decisions made along the way -- not any single new tool.

teaching_blocks.content: The finished analysis now needs to be turned into something the operations team can act on: a narrated stakeholder summary of what was found.

Designing a communication with a specific person in mind, even if that isn't always the reality, can help avoid treating a 'mixed audience' as one undifferentiated group; knowing what motivates that audience lets you frame what you need them to know or do in those terms. So instead of writing for 'the ops team' in general, the capstone summary is written as if for the Head of Operations specifically, framing the zone-delay finding around what would motivate that person -- meeting the delivery-time target.

A summary can follow a story structure with an obvious beginning, middle, and end: the beginning level-sets the audience with the big picture and background context, the middle presents what the analysis found, and the ending gives the key takeaway, such as a recommended next step. For the capstone, that means opening with the courier company and last quarter's delivery-time target, then the finding that certain zones are missing it and by how much, then closing with a recommended next step -- though depending on the audience and relationship, that recommendation can instead be placed up front for a Head of Operations who prefers the bottom line first.

During delivery, insights are communicated to the people who need them, sufficiently for them to determine whether the work meets their requirements; this communication can include summary packs, reports, or presentations. For the capstone, that means the finished summary pack should let the Head of Operations judge for themselves whether it actually answers the zone-delay question they raised, not just report that the analysis was done.
A narrated summary aimed at one specific person, moving through beginning, middle, and end, is what turns the capstone's findings into something its audience can actually use.

teaching_blocks.content: The very last capstone step: package the finished work so someone who never watched it get built can understand and evaluate it.

Transparency about the analytical decisions, process, limitations, and changes made at each stage should be clearly shown through documentation of the analysis, assumptions, and data, together with records of the decisions and quality-assurance checks made. For the capstone, that means documenting things like how missing delivery-time values were handled, what 'last quarter' was defined as, and the checks run to confirm the Orders/Drivers keys matched correctly.

Delivery and communication activities can include producing summary packs and reports, launching dashboards or websites, and giving presentations. The capstone's deliverable is the finished report or summary pack, together with the visualization set already built, presented to the operations team that raised the original question.

Documenting the decisions made and presenting the finished report and visuals together is what makes the capstone a deliverable someone else can evaluate, rather than just finished work only you understand.
